newsitem.title: UK: Softer UK credit will not quieten rate rise calls.
newsitem.headline: Softer UK credit will not quieten rate rise calls.

text.p: A monthly dip in British personal borrowing in March provides some evidence that the consumer-led recovery is not getting out of hand, but it will not quieten calls for a rate rise soon after the May 1 election.
Consumer credit grew by 780 million pounds in March, the lowest rise since June last year, and compares with a massive 1.192 billion rise in February.

"The slowdown in credit is welcome but inevitable after February's huge surge. The March monthly rise is still only in line with recent numbers," said Andrew Snowball, UK economist at the Co-operative Bank. "It doesn't change much in terms of the outlook after the election where the consumer-led expansion will continue and interest rates will rise."
Britain's economic recovery has been driven by consumer spending which has, in turn, been fuelled by income tax cuts and windfall payouts from building society flotations.

But the underlying trend in personal borrowing has shown some signs of softening, suggesting higher wealth is not likely to trigger a runaway consumer boom. "The figures suggest consumer are certainly feeling sufficiently confident to take on more debt," said Dharshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
"But the trend has flattened off in recent months so we are unlikely to see borrowing become as reckless as in the late 1980s."

The three month growth rate slowed slightly in March with the three-month annualised rate up 16 percent compared with 17.3 percent in February. The year-on-year rise slowed to 17.1 percent in March from 17.4 percent in February.

But despite this slower trend -- and only a modest rise in retail sales in the month -- economists still expect the next Chancellor of the Exchequer to come under pressure from Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George to raise interest rates promptly.
Bank officials are likely to argue that year-on-year economic growth of 3.0 percent is inconsistent with the inflation target of 2.5 percent.
The authorities will meet on May 7 and, if the opinion polls are right, opposition Labour's finance spokesman Gordon Brown will face George at the Treasury.
But Snowball does not expect Brown to raise rates at this first meeting.

"Gordon Brown will not be any more keen than Kenneth Clarke was to raise interest rates and it will be easy for him to resist George's call for a rate rise at the first meeting." He said Brown can argue that he has not had time to weigh up all the evidence on the economy yet.
And, as Brown will be in the early stages of drawing up plans for the mini-budget, he can also say he wants to consider fiscal and monetary policy together.
"But I think we'll get a quarter point rate rise by June or July with another quarter point rise later on in the year."
